meta.title: Use of Laboratory Thermometer in Pharmacognosy Laboratory

sections.purpose: To accurately measure temperature in pharmacognosy experiments including water baths, extraction processes, drying operations, and storage areas to ensure process control and sample integrity.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmacognosy laboratory for all temperature measurement operations in equipment verification, extraction monitoring, and storage condition recording.
procedure: Select the correct thermometer range for the application: 0–100°C for water baths and general use; 0–250°C for high-temperature operations (oven, heating mantle); −20 to +40°C for cold storage monitoring.
Inspect the thermometer for visible damage: cracks in the glass, separation of the liquid column (for mercury/spirit thermometers), or error codes (for digital thermometers).
For liquid-in-glass thermometers with a separated column: carefully warm the bulb in your hand or briefly in warm water to rejoin the column before use.
Immerse the thermometer to at least the immersion mark (usually indicated by a ring or '76 mm' mark on the stem) into the medium being measured — partial immersion gives significantly wrong readings.
Allow at least 2–3 minutes for the thermometer to reach thermal equilibrium with the medium before reading.
Read the temperature at eye level with the meniscus (for mercury: read the top of the mercury column; for spirit/alcohol: read the bottom of the meniscus).
For digital thermometers: simply read the stable display value after equilibration.
Record the temperature to the nearest 0.1°C for precise measurements.
After use, remove from the medium and allow to cool before cleaning — do not plunge hot thermometers into cold liquid (thermal shock causes breakage).
Clean with a damp cloth or appropriate solvent; store in a protective case vertically.
Record thermometer ID, reading, date, and application in the laboratory register.
Calibrate annually against a NIST-traceable reference thermometer using ice water (0°C) and boiling water (100°C at sea level) as two-point check.
precautions: Handle glass thermometers with great care — breakage releases mercury (toxic) or spirit (flammable); broken thermometers must be cleaned up per hazardous material protocol.
Never use a mercury thermometer near open flames — mercury is extremely toxic and non-biodegradable; prefer digital or spirit thermometers.
Never use a thermometer as a stirring rod — mechanical stress on the glass causes breakage.
Ensure the thermometer range is appropriate — measuring above the maximum range causes bursting of the bulb reservoir.
Do not leave glass thermometers unsupported horizontally — they bend and break under their own weight at elevated temperatures.
Ensure the immersion depth is correct — partial immersion introduces systematic error of 1–5°C.
Calibrate all thermometers used for official pharmacopeial testing annually.
